Ritu sighed and leaned on the railing. 'My grandmother's not well. We're going to Nagpur this weekend. I didn't want to talk about it.'
'Oh.' Kalyani's face fell. 'I'm sorry. I thought...'

passage: In second year, my friend Afreen went quiet for almost a month. She skipped the canteen, stopped replying in our group chat, and I decided it was because of me. That October I'd forgotten her birthday by a day. I felt so guilty that the guilt itself seemed like proof: nobody feels this bad unless they've done something bad. I, Zubin, wrote her three long apology messages. She answered the third with just, 'Why are you sorry?' Later she told me her parents were going through a rough patch and she'd been going home every weekend. My birthday slip had barely registered. Looking back, the guilt wasn't useless. It told me how much the friendship mattered. It just wasn't evidence. What she needed was someone to sit with her, not someone apologising.

qa.q: By how much had Zubin forgotten Afreen's birthday?
qa.a: Zubin had forgotten her birthday by a day.

qa.q: Why did Zubin's guilt feel like proof?
qa.a: The feeling was so strong that Zubin reasoned nobody feels this bad without doing something bad, so the missed birthday became the cause without any real evidence.

qa.q: What would have helped more than three apology messages?
qa.a: Asking Afreen gently how she was, and simply spending time with her, would have met her real need instead of centring Zubin's guilt.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt receiving three long apologies?
qa.a: Afreen was likely confused and a little tired, since she was dealing with trouble at home and the missed birthday had barely registered, which is why she asked 'Why are you sorry?'

grounding: Shows a student looking back on assuming a friend's month of low mood was their fault because the guilt felt so strong.

We talked about asking the roommate kindly how she is doing, and mentioning that the counselling cell is open to her too. Alka left calmer. Jasleen, counsellor

passage: The 8:10 local stopped dead between Dadar and Matunga, and Kamal's big meeting with Rukmini, the head of procurement, was at nine. His chest tightened. His palms were damp on the folder. The thought arrived fully formed: this is going to go terribly. He noticed it the way you notice a cough. Okay. I feel anxious. That's a feeling about the meeting, not the meeting. He messaged Rukmini: 'Train stuck, may be ten minutes late. Can start by phone if easier.' Then he opened his notes and went over his three points, one for each station he couldn't see. At 9:02 Rukmini called. Kamal stood by the door of the packed compartment, one hand on the rail, heart still going fast, and began with point one.

qa.a: The 8:10 local stopped dead between Dadar and Matunga.

passage: Madhuri reached the Sector 17 office forty minutes early for her first appraisal meeting and sat in the pantry holding a cup of tea she didn't drink. Fact: finished all four projects, two early. She looked at it. 'The first line is true. The second line is also true. Only one of them is about the meeting.' Gurpreet grinned. 'So what's the plan?' 'Same plan. Walk in, show the four projects, ask about the lead role.' Her stomach still fluttered on the way to the cabin. She went in anyway.

passage: I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's cousin, and we share a room when he stays with us in the holidays. Chinmay is ten, and he has rules. He told me them once: always come first, never cry. When his unit test came back with 46 out of 50, and a girl in his class had 48, he didn't come down for dinner. I found him under the blanket, very still. I think he was crying, but when I asked, he said, 'I'm not. I don't cry.' Later I saw him writing the rules again on a sticky note, pressing so hard the pen tore the paper. I don't know everything he was feeling. But 46 is a good mark, and he looked like he'd done something terrible.

passage: Yamini, you've rubbed out that answer so many times the page is thin. When I was your age, in a village school near Nashik, I made myself two rules. Ramesh must always be first in class. Ramesh must never cry. I said them every morning like a prayer. One year a new boy came and beat me in arithmetic by two marks. I didn't eat that evening. When my eyes started to water, I went behind the cowshed so no one would see, and I felt ashamed of the marks and ashamed of the tears, both together. My Aaji found me there. She didn't scold. She just asked, 'Who made these rules, you or God?' I had no answer. It took me years to loosen them. Don't take so long.

qa.a: Ramesh went behind the cowshed so no one would see.

qa.a: Both broke Ramesh's own rules, always first and never cry, so losing by just two marks felt like a double failure.

qa.a: Ramesh is showing the rules from the outside, with Aaji's question, so Yamini can notice the rubbed-out answer and ask who made the rules before they harden.

passage: Looking back at Class 11, I think I was angry with almost everyone. My parents should have understood that I hated science without me saying it. Lalremsiami, my best friend, should have been free every Saturday, because that's what best friends are. When she started badminton coaching on weekends, I didn't say anything. I just got colder. I left her messages on read. I told myself she should notice. She did notice, eventually, and asked me outside the library, 'Damini, what did I do?' And I realised I'd never actually told her anything. Not about the Saturdays, not about how lonely they had got. The resentment had grown for months; the conversation took ten minutes. We moved our plans to Sunday evenings. I still catch myself thinking 'should' about people. Now it's my cue to say something.

qa.a: Lalremsiami asked outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Damini get colder instead of speaking up?
qa.a: Damini believed a best friend should just notice and be free, so saying it out loud felt like it shouldn't be needed, and the hurt turned into resentment instead.

qa.q: What does Damini do now when a 'should' thought appears, and why does it help?
qa.a: Damini treats the 'should' as a cue to say something, which catches resentment early and gives the other person a real chance to respond.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami before that talk outside the library?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt confused and shut out, watching a friend turn cold without knowing why, which is why she finally asked straight out.

Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday
Gautam has seemed irritable all week, snapping at his group during the science project. Today he stayed back and let it out. His parents 'should understand' that he wants to switch to commerce; his friends 'should be there, every single time' for the project, and two of them went to a cousin's wedding instead. When I asked whether he had told his parents about commerce, he said, 'They should know. It's obvious.' He had not told them. He had not told his friends that the deadline worried him, either. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write three things he wished people knew, and next to each, one person he could tell. He wrote 'Papa' next to commerce. Nikita
